title: A limited memory algorithm for bound constrained optimization
contribution: Second read (inc-ocr) of L-BFGS-B, the algorithm paper: parameter values, cost formulas and Tables 1-3. At m = 5, L-BFGS-B fails on 4 of 34 CUTE bound problems (LANCELOT-SR1 on 0), needs more evaluations than LANCELOT on almost every row, and takes less time than both LANCELOT options on 12 of the 15 problems with n >= 100.
problem_entry: As in the c02 card: min f s.t. l <= x <= u, gradient only, storage linear in n (p. 2); per-iteration cost of order n through compact limited-memory matrices (p. 3).
key_idea: B = theta I - W M W' with W = [Y theta S], M 2m x 2m (p. 5); theta = y'y/y's, B0 = I (p. 18); line search alpha = 1e-4, beta = 0.9, unit step first, More-Thuente with max step to the closest bound (pp. 4, 18-19); skip pair unless s'y > eps|y|^2, eps = 2.2e-16 (pp. 6, 18). Cauchy point: first segment O(n), later segments O(m^2) each (Remark p. 9), total (2m+2)n + O(m^2) n_int + n log n (p. 10). Subspace: direct primal 2m^2 t + 6mt + 4t + O(m^3) (5.12) (p. 13); CG stop |r| < min(0.1, sqrt|r_c|)|r_c|, cost (2m+2)t + (4m+6)t citer + O(m^2), cheaper than direct only if citer < m/2, at most 2m iterations (pp. 14-15); dual (2m+3)n + 9m t_a + 2m^2 t_a + O(m^3), primal brought to 2m^2 t_a + 6mt + 4t + O(m^3) by the primal-dual identity (pp. 17-18).
assumptions: Smooth f, gradient only, simple bounds; B_k positive definite gives g'd < 0 (p. 4); no convergence analysis (p. 4).
proof_devices: no theorems; descent from m_k(x_k) > m_k(x_c) >= m_k(x_bar) (p. 4)
breakpoint recursion (4.9)-(4.12) carried by p = W'd and c = W'z, O(m^2) per segment (pp. 8-10)
operation counts for direct primal (5.12), CG (5.14) and dual, with the crossover citer < m/2 (pp. 13, 15, 17)
saved inner products and Y'ZZ'Y = Y'Y - Y'AA'Y when t >> n - t (p. 13)
primal-dual matrix identity reducing the primal cost to the dual's (pp. 17-18)
experiments: Both codes stop at |P(x-g,l,u)-x|_inf < 1e-5 (p. 18); SPARCstation 2, 40 MHz, 32 MB; F1 = not solved in 999 evaluations, F2 = indistinguishable next iterate (p. 19); discard n < 4, yet HS25 (n = 3) is tabulated (pp. 19-22). Table 1 (p. 20, 34 problems): failures m=5 4, m=17 2, LANCELOT-BFGS 5 F1, LANCELOT-SR1 0; JNLBRNGA 313/843.59 vs SR1 24/1474.09, OBSTCLAE 282/277.71 vs 7/1763.42, OBSTCLBM 133/383.61 vs 7/1275.72, TORSION6 301/835.80 vs 10/168.67; card writer's count n >= 100: m=5 faster than both LANCELOT options on 12 of 15, slower on JNLBRNGB and TORSION6, F1 on BQPGAUSS; fewer evaluations than SR1 on 3 of 34 rows. Table 2 (p. 21, m = 3/5/17/29): failures 3/4/2/2; TORSION6 time 646.21/835.80/1582.75/2442.59, nfg 298/301/400/385; no comment in the text. Table 3 (p. 22, primal/dual/cg vs LANCELOT Hessian): failures 4/4/1/0; dual 5-19% slower on the four largest, cg 1.9x on JNLBRNGA and 1.7x on OBSTCLBM; LANCELOT-Hessian nf 22/6/6/9 vs 313/282/133/301, time 1775.51/1696.45/2300.28/150.15 vs 843.59/277.71/383.61/835.80; primal faster on 12 of 15 rows with n >= 100 (card writer's count).
positioning: As in c02; LANCELOT SBMIN run in three options (BFGS, SR1, exact Hessian), each at default settings (p. 19).
writing: As in c02; 'To our surprise' (p. 23) sized by the table: LANCELOT-Hessian takes 2.1x, 6.1x and 6.0x the time of L-BFGS-B on JNLBRNGA, OBSTCLAE and OBSTCLBM (card writer's ratios, p. 22).
limits_future: As in c02; 4 of 34 runs fail at m = 5 (p. 20); evaluation counts 13-47 times LANCELOT's on the largest problems (card writer's ratios, pp. 20, 22); TORSION6 5-5.6x slower than LANCELOT is not singled out in the closing time verdict (pp. 20, 22-23).

method_links.note: One projected-gradient stopping test at 1e-5 for both codes; every non-converged run printed as F1 or F2 and counted as a failure in the text ('three more failures for the cg method'). Correction for 09 #method-1 Say-do and 08 section 2.1, which group S003 with the C1 non-failure accounting: S003 has no C1 marker; it first appears in the December 1994 code report [S005 pp. 9-11].
Rival at default settings in three options; own side in seven configurations (m = 3, 5, 17, 29; primal, dual, cg).
As in c02, with values: pair skipped when s'y <= 2.2e-16 |y|^2 without deleting the oldest; backtracking replaced by More-Thuente (1e-4, 0.9) with the maximum step at the closest bound.
The undecided subspace method is costed three ways ((5.12), (5.14), dual count); Table 3 splits the verdict (cg fewest failures at m = 5, most time) and the text overrules it with other m values.
Two-sided verdict as in c02, with the evaluation gap now sized: 13-47x more evaluations than LANCELOT on the largest problems, but less time on 12 of 15 problems with n >= 100.

transferable: Give alternative inner solvers operation counts in the same units and derive their crossover (citer < m/2) before testing (pp. 13, 15).
Report the tested code's parameter values next to the algorithm statement (alpha = 1e-4, beta = 0.9, eps = 2.2e-16, theta = y'y/y's) (p. 18).
Define each failure marker on the page and count all of them as failures in the text (pp. 19, 23).
Show the memory parameter's trade-off (failures against time over m = 3-29) in one table (p. 21).
Correction for technique catalog D3: in the generalized Cauchy point search each segment after the first costs O(m^2), not O(m) (Remark p. 9; Algorithm CP p. 10).
coauthors: Richard H. Byrd (Colorado), Peihuang Lu, Ciyou Zhu (Northwestern)

title: Algorithm 778: L-BFGS-B: Fortran subroutines for large-scale bound-constrained optimization
contribution: Second read (inc-ocr) of the L-BFGS-B code paper (December 31, 1994 report version): every documented parameter value, the code's skip test and recovery trigger, and Tables 1.1-1.6. At m = 5, 5 of 33 bound runs end F1 and 3 of 34 unconstrained runs are C1 (not counted as failures); the code is faster than both LANCELOT options on 16 of 33 bound and 21 of 34 unconstrained problems.
problem_entry: As in c02; storage about (12 + 2m)n, iteration cost from 4mn + n to about m^2 n multiplications, 8 more n-vectors than L-BFGS (p. 2).
key_idea: Reverse-communication package of S003. m: below 3 not recommended, 3 <= m <= 20 recommended (p. 3); factr test (f_k - f_k+1)/max(|f_k+1|, |f_k|, 1) <= factr*epsmch with factr 1.d+12 / 1.d+7 / 1.d+1, factr = 0 stops only if f unchanged (p. 4); wa (2m+4)n + 12m^2 + 12m, iwa 3n (p. 4); isbmin 1 (default primal) / 2 dual / 3 CG (p. 5); counters isave(26) skipped updates, isave(30), isave(34), dsave(2), dsave(13) (pp. 5, 7). Changes from S003: primal and dual through the inverse of one 2m x 2m indefinite block matrix factorized by Cholesky of its blocks (p. 8); skip test y's/(-g's) <= epsmch (p. 7) instead of S003's s'y > eps|y|^2; second stop at |proj g|_inf = 0 (p. 6).
assumptions: As in c02; epsmch enters only the factr test and the skip test; invariance under scalar multiples of variables and objective except the first iteration and the factr test (p. 7).
proof_devices: no proofs; recovery: after 20 line-search evaluations without sufficient decrease, discard all pairs and restart along steepest descent; second failure gives ABNORMAL TERMINATION IN LINE SEARCH (pp. 6-7)
same restart for a singular or indefinite L-BFGS matrix or submatrix and for g'd >= 0 (p. 7)
one block-matrix inverse shared by the primal and dual subspace computations (p. 8)
experiments: CUTE bound problems with n >= 5 and unconstrained with n >= 100; LANCELOT SR1 and exact Hessian at all defaults; Sparcstation-2 32 Mb; |proj g|_inf <= 1e-5 (p. 8). Markers *, **, C1, F1, C2, F2 relative to LANCELOT-SR1 (pp. 10-11). Table 1.1 (p. 10, 33 bound): m=5 five *F1 (BQPGAUSS, PALMER1E-4E, 9999 limit), m=17 one *C1, LANCELOT none; card writer's count: m=5 faster than both LANCELOT options on 16, tie 1, slower 11, F1 5; never fewer evaluations than LANCELOT-Hessian; JNLBRNGA 332/740.33 vs 24/1263.77 vs 22/1502.96, OBSTCLAE 258/207.20 vs 7/1442.00 vs 6/1422.62, OBSTCLBM 146/353.04 vs 7/1106.37 vs 6/2017.70, TORSION6 362/707.22 vs 10/130.73 vs 9/130.31. Table 1.2 (p. 11, 34 unconstrained): m=5 **C1 on FLETCHBV, FREUROTH, PENALTY3; LANCELOT-SR1 *F2 FLETCHBV, C2 NONDIA; LANCELOT-Hessian *F1 FLETCHBV, **C1 PENALTY3; m=5 faster on 21, slower on 10 (DIXMAANI 166.37 vs 9.30, TRIDIA 48.90 vs 3.91); fewer evaluations than Hessian only on NONDIA and PENALTY1. Table 1.3 (p. 12): bound F1 runs 7/5/0/0 for m = 3/5/17/29; TORSION6 time 565.25/707.22/1157.74/1994.78. Table 1.4 (p. 13): C1 runs 3/3/4/3, no F1. Tables 1.5-1.6 (pp. 14-15): dual and CG have the same five F1 at m=5; CG m=5 1419.78 s on JNLBRNGA (primal 740.33); CG m=17 DIXMAANI 1679.64 s (primal 273.08). Evaluation limit 9999 here vs 999 in S003; MAXLIKA F1 in S003 at m=5 converges here in 1665 evaluations (card writer's comparison).
positioning: As in c02; larger CUTE instances than S003 (n = 1000/1024 for BDEXP, MCCORMCK, NONSCOMP, TORSION1-4, OBSTCL*L/U against 10-100 in S003) (p. 10; S003 p. 20).
writing: As in c02; advice as numbers (m range p. 3; factr values p. 4; isbmin default p. 5).
limits_future: As in c02; five F1 runs of 33 at m = 5 on bound problems (p. 10); the good-f, unmet-gradient-test behaviour is 3 of 34 unconstrained runs at m = 5 (p. 11) and 'deserves further study' (p. 9).

method_links.note: Kept from c02, now sized: C1 runs (test missed, f at least as good as LANCELOT-SR1's) are not counted as failures. They are 3 of 34 unconstrained runs at m = 5 and 5 of 67 at m = 17. The marking is also applied to the rival (LANCELOT-Hessian **C1 on PENALTY3; both LANCELOT options fail on FLETCHBV), and all five bound misses at m = 5 are printed as F1.
One stopping test, |proj g|_inf <= 1e-5, for all codes.
isbmin with default 1; driver4 runs 67 problems x 3 options; Tables 1.5-1.6 publish all three options.
Step 4 only, with values: restart after 20 failed line-search evaluations, then a named exit; no estimate drives the repair.

Drawback (iii), structure cannot be used (p. 3); at m = 5 more evaluations than LANCELOT-Hessian on 27 of 28 converged bound rows (tie on HS110) and 28 of 31 converged unconstrained rows (card writer's count).

transferable: Ship a stopping-tolerance table in words and numbers (factr 1.d+12 / 1.d+7 / 1.d+1) for a stated machine precision (p. 4).
Define failure markers relative to a reference code and apply them to every column, the rival's other options included (pp. 10-11).
Give the user counters for every recovery device (skipped updates in isave(26)) (p. 7).
Put a numeric bound on a recovery trigger (20 evaluations without sufficient decrease) and document the second-failure exit (pp. 6-7).
When the code's safeguard differs from the algorithm paper's (skip test), print the code's version in the software paper (p. 7).
Heuristic 2 evidence: user-readable counters (pp. 5, 7); Heuristic 5 variant: m range 3 <= m <= 20 (p. 3) against the 1989 '3<= M <=7' cited in SKILL.md.
coauthors: Ciyou Zhu, Richard H. Byrd (Colorado), Peihuang Lu

quotes.text: It runs the code on 67 test problems (33 bound constrained, 34 unconstrained) from the CUTE collection
If the line search is unable to find a point with a sufficiently lower value of the objective after 20 evaluations of the objective function, we conclude that the current direction is not useful

title: Large scale unconstrained optimization
contribution: Second read (inc-ocr) of the 1996 single-author survey: numeric recipes (LANCELOT 11-band preconditioner, Minpack-2 shift rule, m in [3, 20]) and Tables 1-3. His limited-memory codes lose to LANCELOT's Newton in evaluations on 7 of 8 rows and win in time on 5 of 8. The rows are the m = 5 and LANCELOT-Hessian entries of S005's tables.
problem_entry: As in the c03 card; n large, 'say n > 500' (p. 2).
key_idea: Partial separability f = sum phi_i(U_i x) (2.8)-(2.9), minimum-surface element on 4 variables with 3 distinct Hessian elements and invariant subspace of dimension n - 2 (pp. 3-4); Algorithm I CG trust-region step with three exits (p. 8); LANCELOT default 11-band modified Cholesky (p. 9); Minpack-2 shift alpha0 = 0 or beta/2, alpha_k+1 = max(2 alpha_k, beta/2) after diagonal scaling (p. 10); residual test |r_j+1| <= eps|r_0| (3.6) or eps(|B||p| + |r_0|) (p. 11); L-BFGS H0 = gamma I with gamma = s'y/y'y, m in [3, 20] (p. 14); compact form (4.10)-(4.12) (pp. 15-16); strong Wolfe 0 < sigma1 < sigma2 < 1/2 and beta = max{beta_PR, 0} for CG (pp. 19-20).
assumptions: As in c03; CG results assume a bounded level set, a Lipschitz gradient nearby and no restarts (p. 19).
proof_devices: survey, no proofs; monotone CG iterate norms 0 = |p0| < ... < |pj| < |pj+1| ... <= Delta and the Cauchy first iterate (p. 9)
PR with the new line search of [36]: liminf |g_k| = 0 (5.6) (p. 19)
global convergence for 0 <= beta_k <= beta_FR [64] and any |beta_k| <= beta_FR [30], tight for some c > 1 (p. 20)
sparse quasi-Newton update unique under linear independence; 2 pairs suffice for an arrowhead matrix (pp. 17-18)
experiments: Table 1 (p. 10, Bouaricha-More's results): GL2 n = 2,500/10,000/40,000 iterations 6/6/8, evaluations 12/10/12, time 13.0/63.4/537.7; MSA 6/6/10, 7/7/14, 2.8/2.8/91.1; card writer's arithmetic: 16x n gives 41x (GL2) and 33x (MSA) time, MSA time at 10,000 equals that at 2,500, against 'only a little faster than linearly'. Table 2 (p. 15, L-BFGS m=5 vs LANCELOT Newton defaults, nfg/time): CRAGGLVY 95/13 vs 15/10, FMINSURF 186/11 vs 316/106, DIXMAANI 1237/166 vs 8/9, EIGENCLS 2900/563 vs 543/2300. Table 3 (p. 16, L-BFGS-B): JNLBRNGA 332/740 vs 22/1503, LINVERSE 291/57 vs 28/150, OBSTCLAE 258/207 vs 6/1423, TORSION6 362/707 vs 9/130. Card writer's count: more evaluations on 7 of 8 rows, less time on 5 of 8. Table 3 and three Table 2 rows are the rounded S005 Table 1.1-1.2 entries (S005 pp. 10-11); in S005's 34 unconstrained problems L-BFGS-B needs fewer evaluations than LANCELOT-Hessian on 2. TORSION6 (LANCELOT 5.4x faster) is passed over by the time verdict (p. 17).
positioning: As in c03; tables come from his group's report [65] and Bouaricha-More [7] (pp. 10, 14, 16).
writing: As in c03; rows chosen because they 'typify situations we have observed in practice' (p. 15).
limits_future: As in c03; four rows per table, no aggregate, although the aggregate exists in S005 and is not summarised (pp. 15-16).

method_links.note: Refines SKILL.md Method 6 and 09 #taste-marks mark 6 ('shown losing to Newton and partitioned quasi-Newton'): in the tables his codes lose to LANCELOT's Newton in evaluations on 7 of 8 rows but win in time on 5 of 8; the loss to partially separable quasi-Newton is asserted in prose without numbers (pp. 13-14). Holds for evaluations and reliability, not for time.
Rival at all default settings, L-BFGS at m = 5; rows are a declared selection from a larger table (S005) cited but not summarised.
As in c03: CG convergence results stated with conditions and judged by practical effect ('only a marginal improvement'; no significant practical advances).
As in c03: open-question subsections per algorithm class.

transferable: Report the full numeric recipe of a preconditioner shift (alpha0 = 0 or beta/2, alpha_k+1 = max(2 alpha_k, beta/2)) (p. 10).
Check a printed growth claim ('a little faster than linearly') against the ratios in the table before printing it (p. 10).
Tie illustrative rows to their source table and its aggregate (pp. 15-16; S005 pp. 10-11).
Heuristic 5 variant: m in [3, 20] (p. 14), wider than the 1989 '3<= M <=7' cited in SKILL.md.
coauthors: none (sole author on the title page, p. 1)

quotes.text: The memory parameter for L-BFGS was set to m = 5, and LANCELOT was run with all its default settings
These are very good results in that the number of iterations stays nearly constant as the dimension of the problem increases, and computing time grows only a little faster than linearly

title: Combining trust region and line search techniques
contribution: Second read (inc-ocr) of the trust-region/backtracking hybrid with Yuan: the equations of Algorithm 2.6 and 3.1, the lemma and theorem statements (liminf |g_k| = 0 under sum 1/M_k = infinity, M_k = 1 + max|B_i|), and Tables I-II. Function evaluations over 18 MGH problems are 1125 (line search), 986 (pure TR) and 999 (TR+BT); SR1 beats BFGS on all 8 medium problems.
problem_entry: As in c03; re-solving (B_k + lambda I)d = -g_k (1.4) after a failed step is costly for large n (p. 2).
key_idea: d(lambda) = -(B + lambda I)^-1 g (2.29), accepted if Delta/gamma <= |d| <= Delta with gamma > 1 (2.30) or if lambda <= |B| + (1+eps)|g|/Delta (2.33) and |d| <= Delta (2.34); both give (2.37)-(2.38) with tau = min{1/8, 1/2gamma} (pp. 8-10). Algorithm 2.6: lambda := lambda + (|d|^2/|q|^2)(gamma|d| - Delta)/Delta (2.39), Newton on 1/|d| - gamma/Delta (2.40) instead of More-Sorensen's (2.41) (p. 10). Algorithm 3.1: backtrack f(x + alpha^i d) < f(x) (3.3), curved paths with |d(i+1)| in [alpha1, alpha2]|d(i)| and the cosine condition (3.4)-(3.5) (p. 11); 0 < c3 < c4 < 1 < c1, 0 < c2 < 1, Delta_k+1 in [|x_k+1 - x_k|, c4 Delta_k] after backtracking (3.8) (p. 12). Runs: gamma = 1.5; Wolfe 0.01/0.9; BFGS skipped if s'y <= 0; SR1 only if |s'y| >= 1e-6|s||y|; alpha_k = max{0.1, 0.5/[1 + (f(x) - f(x+d))/d'g]}; Delta1 = 1, B1 = I, stop |g| <= 1e-8; c1-c4 and eps not reported (pp. 19-20). Corrections for c03: the interval constant is gamma, not tau; M_k carries '1 +'.
assumptions: Assumptions 3.2: iterates in a closed convex set S, f twice differentiable with |Hessian| <= M (3.12)-(3.13) (p. 13); B_k only through M_k = 1 + max_{1<=i<=k}|B_i| (3.19) with sum 1/M_k = infinity (3.43) (pp. 13, 17).
proof_devices: Lemma 2.3: 0 <= lambda* <= |g|/Delta - sigma_n(B) and d*'g <= -|g|^2/(sigma_1 - sigma_n + |g|/Delta) (2.14)-(2.15) (pp. 5-6)
Lemma 2.5: cos(d_Delta1, -g) >= cos(d_Delta2, -g) for Delta2 > Delta1, three cases incl. the hard case (pp. 7-8)
Lemmas 3.3-3.5: Delta_k bounded below by a constant times min{mu(1 - c2), 1}/M_k for ratio failures and backtracking (pp. 14-17)
Lemma 3.6 (Powell 1984) sequence lemma; Theorem 3.7 liminf |g_k| = 0 under sum 1/M_k = infinity (pp. 17-18)
Corollary 3.8 (Newton): liminf, lim |g_k| = 0 for convex f, PSD Hessian at a limit, quadratic rate (3.47) (p. 18)
experiments: Table I (p. 21, 18 MGH problems, n = 2-20): card writer's sums: function evaluations 1125 (line-search BFGS), 986 (pure TR), 999 (TR+BT BFGS); gradient evaluations 902, 986, 864; iterations 821, 986, 864. TR+BT BFGS fewer iterations than pure TR on 13, equal 3, more 2 (problems 5, 8); function evaluations fewer 5, equal 5, more 8. TR+BT SR1 > 300 iterations on problems 4 and 12. The text compares in function evaluations only; in gradient evaluations line search (902) beats pure TR (986), not stated. Table II (p. 22, Liu-Nocedal problems 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 15, 16; n = 50-121): SR1 fewer iterations and evaluations than BFGS on all 8; BFGS > 300 on problem 7; other 7: 699 vs 1107 function evaluations (card writer's sums). No run above n = 121.
writing: As in c03; comparative convergence claim 'as strong as the results obtained previously for pure trust region methods' (p. 19).
limits_future: As in c03; no test above n = 121 although large n motivates the paper (pp. 2, 21-22); update ranking reverses between tables (pp. 21-22); trust-region constants of the runs unreported (pp. 19-20).

method_links.note: Theorem 3.7 needs only sum 1/M_k = infinity (at most linear growth of |B_k|), set against the condition-number or trace-determinant control of line-search quasi-Newton theory; Corollary 3.8 gives the four Newton conclusions incl. the quadratic rate.
Four arms in one Fortran code with Delta1 = 1, B1 = I, |g| <= 1e-8; evaluations counted per arm.
Headline measure: line search vs pure TR ranked in function evaluations (1125 vs 986); gradient evaluations (902 vs 986) would reverse it (card writer's sums); both counts are printed.
Surprise reversal, now complete in numbers: SR1 wins all 8 medium problems after losing to BFGS in Table I.
As in c03: one component changed (re-solve -> backtrack), triggered by cost, no estimate or recovery tree.

transferable: Solve the trust-region subproblem by Newton's method on 1/|d(lambda)| - gamma/Delta, accepting any |d| in [Delta/gamma, Delta]; only positive definite factorizations are needed ((2.39)-(2.41), p. 10).
Certify the inequalities the fallback needs ((2.37)-(2.38), tau = min{1/8, 1/2gamma}) inside the inexact subproblem solver (p. 10).
Carry one growth scalar M_k = 1 + max|B_i| through the convergence proof (pp. 13-18).
Total iterations, f and g per arm and check whether the ranking flips between counts (pp. 20-21).
Print every constant of the tested configuration next to its equation; here c1-c4 are missing (pp. 19-20).

quotes.text: We tested the algorithms on the 18 examples given by Moré, Garbow and Hillstrom (1981)
the pure trust region methods requires fewer function evaluations, but the difference is not significant
